item.title: Image-Charge Barriers, Not Polaron Kinetics, Limit Charge Extraction at Ligand-Passivated CsPbI3 Interfaces
item.description:
Charge extraction across inorganic perovskite–organic ligand interfaces represents a critical materials bottleneck in perovskite optoelectronics, yet the defectindependent electrostatic origins of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we present a multiscale framework that combines first-principles density functional theory with macroscopic Scharfetter–Gummel drift-diffusion simulations to isolate and quantify this intrinsic transport barrier on CsPbI3 surfaces passivated by methylammonium (MA), butylammonium (BA), and phenethylammonium (PEA). We demonstrate that effective interfacial dielectric screening is governed by ligand orientational polarizability and adsorption geometry rather than isolated molecular polarizability, producing a counter-intuitive ordering εBA > εMA > εPEA that inverts the conventional molecular polarizability sequence. The resulting imagecharge barriers (Umax im = 202.6–229.8 meV) exceed kBT by nearly an order of magnitude, driving severe thermodynamic carrier depletion (CAF = 1.38 × 10−4–3.95 × 10−4), while all computed polaron reorganization energies (λ < 100 meV) confirm delocalized, large-polaron character—unambiguously establishing that the dominant bottleneck is electrostatic rather than kinetic. Despite its lowest electron reorganization energy (λe = 37.8 meV), PEA’s orientational locking generates the largest image-charge barrier (Umax im = 229.8 meV), whereas the conformationally flexible BA maximizes in-plane screening and reduces steady-state carrier accumulation by an order of magnitude under operational bias. Furthermore, ligand rigidity governs a structural electron–hole reorganization asymmetry (λh/λe = 0.98–1.85), establishing a defect-independent, purely structural mechanism for carrier selectivity. These findings deliver four quantitative design rules for charge-transparent passivation interlayers, replacing empirical ligand screening with a predictive framework anchored in orientational polarizability, adsorption geometry, and carrier-type symmetry. The identified image-charge barrier constitutes a Boltzmann activation energy Uim(T ) that is directly measurable via temperature-dependent photoconductance, providing an unambiguous experimental validation signature.

Naveen Kumar, Anirban Mondal

item.title: Reactive Machine-Learned Potentials Improve Predictions of Water Diffusion Behaviour in Defective Industrial Zeolite HY
item.description:
Dealuminated HY (USY) zeolites are of major industrial catalytic importance, and the defects they contain, such as extraframework aluminum (EFAL) and silanol groups, strongly influence the behaviour of adsorbed species. Here, we show that reactive neural network-based machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) provide a substantial improvement in the simulation of water diffusion in these catalysts. They yield markedly improved agreement with quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) measurements of mobility for models of intact framework regions, refined further once EFAL and silanol defects are included explicitly, capturing the additional hindrance these sites impose on water motion. The ability of MLIPs to generate and stabilise realistic defect structures constitutes a step change in the molecular level and nanoscale modelling of industrial zeolites. This combined capability enables the quantitative investigation of defect-specific effects on nanoscale diffusion and provides a new approach for accurately modelling transport in industrially relevant zeolite catalysts.

Indranil Saha, Alexander James Porter, Andreas Erlebach, Jacques Ollivier, Christopher J. Heard, Alexander James O’Malley, Lukáš Grajciar

item.title: Calcium Poly(heptazine imide): Reproducible Synthesis for Structural Analysis, Mechanism of CO <sub>2</sub> Uptake, and Evaluation of Photocatalytic CO <sub>2</sub> - to-CO Conversion
item.description:
The framework material, calcium poly(heptazine imide) or CaPHI, is reportedly capable for CO 2 absorption, although harsh conditions from literature synthesis method result in low and unpredictable yield that hinders evaluation of its applicability for CO 2 capture and conversion (CCC). This work presents a synthesis procedure for CaPHI with cross-laboratory reproducibility and scalable to 100s mg by employing a CaCl 2 -based eutectic as synthesis medium. Comprehensive characterization confirmed the PHI structure, with Ca 2+ residing in the structural porosity having ionic conductivity of 10 -10 –10 -11 S cm -1 as estimated by electrochemical measurements. In addition to the literature’s physisorption mechanism for dry CO 2 , we demonstrated these Ca 2+ to participate in direct air capture of humid CO 2 , which chemisorbs as CaCO 3 from structural analyses. For photocatalytic CO 2 -to-CO conversion, CaPHI outperforms its K + -bearing counterpart, which we speculatively attributed to strong Ca 2+ –CO 2 interactions that concentrate this reactant near the active sites. In establishing a reliable synthesis and demonstrating its ability for CO 2 capture and photoreduction, further optimization of CaPHI’s structure, morphology and compositing with co-catalyst could reveal its potential for CCC, while incorporation of mobile Ca 2+ may represent a broad design principle warranting future research for material development for improving the efficiency of carbon capture & utilization.

Chi-Chen Chang, Hsin-Hui Lin, Pin-Yu Shi, Stefan Repp, Bettina V. Lotsch, Wen-Hui Sophia Cheng, Vincent Wing-hei Lau

item.title: Understanding the Relationship Between Synthetic Conditions and H <sub>2</sub> Uptake Capacity in Oxidatively Activated Turbostratic Carbons through Machine Learning
item.description:
The relationship between synthesis parameters, porosity, and H 2 uptake in activated carbons is a field of significant investigation and discussion. Conclusions about these relationships are typically drawn from limited datasets of carbons produced for a given publication, and are not able to consider the interplay between various synthesis parameters and properties of the resultant turbostratic carbons. We present the first attempt at understanding the relationship between synthesis parameters and H 2 uptake capacity in turbostratic carbons, using the single point pore volume as a proxy due to the dearth of available high pressure H 2 isotherms. The methods used herein have exploited a dataset of 237 samples to determine the most important synthesis parameters in determining the porosity of the product and thus their suitability for high pressure H 2 storage applications.

L Scott Blankenship, Filippo Federici Canova, David Gao, Robert Mokaya

item.title: Factorised Cartesian Atomic Cluster Expansion for Low-Cost Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description:
Machine-learning interatomic potentials can reach the accuracy of density functional theory at a fraction of its cost, but the most accurate equivariant models remain expensive, mainly because of the tensor operations they perform for every pair of neighbouring atoms. We present FACE, a factorised Cartesian atomic cluster expansion that removes this bottleneck. Each neighbour contributes only a small set of radial functions and messages, and all mixing of feature channels is done once per atom, so the cost per neighbour no longer grows with the size of the model. Custom GPU kernels evaluate the remaining steps, and long-range electrostatics, dispersion and short-range repulsion attach through a single interface. We show that the training divergences we encountered originate in how the network weights are scaled, and we introduce a distillation scheme in which an ensemble generates additional, uncertainty-checked training data. On five rMD17 molecules, with identical training budgets and hardware, FACE is about as accurate as a 64-channel MACE model (over three seeds: better on one molecule, within the seed spread on two, 7–14% higher force errors on two), while it is 5.7 times faster at inference (4.9 times at the same cutoff) and needs 3.5–3.9 times less GPU memory. Training costs about the same per step. Distillation lowers the energy and force errors of a single aspirin model by 20% at fixed width, to 2.26 meV and 6.74 meV/Å, close to the published MACE values (2.2 and 6.6), and the distilled model runs stably in molecular dynamics.

Albert Linda

item.title: Machine-Learning-Guided Prediction and Statistical Analysis of Electronic Bandgaps in Double-Perovskite Oxides for Photovoltaic and Optoelectronic Design
item.description:
Double-perovskite oxides (A2BB′O6) are attractive for photovoltaic and optoelectronic applications, but their bandgap depends on a compositional space too large for routine DFT screening. In this study, we build composition-only machine-learning models on 1,306 DFTcomputed (GLLB-SC) double perovskites, using 72 descriptors derived from elemental electronegativity, ionic/atomic radius, group and period position, Mendeleev number, and first ionization energy. Six regression algorithms were compared under 10-fold cross-validation where a tuned XGBoost model gave the best results (test R2 = 0.975, MAE = 0.188 eV, RMSE = 0.245 eV), outperforming all others with statistical confidence (Friedman χ2 = 45.14, p =1.4×10-7; Wilcoxon p < 0.005 throughout). SHAP analysis pointed to A-site group number and B-site electronegativity and radius as the main drivers of bandgap, matching the mechanisms reported in the original DFT study. These results demonstrate that interpretable, composition-only machinelearning models can reproduce DFT-level bandgap trends at negligible computational cost, providing a practical high-throughput screening tool for lead-free double-perovskite discovery.

Md Ragib Abid, Md Shafayatul Islam

item.title: Strain-Tunable Electron–Phonon Coupling Collapse in Oxide Perovskites: A First-Principles Route to Suppressed Hot-Carrier Thermalization
item.description:
Hot-carrier thermalization constitutes the dominant energy loss channel in perovskite photovoltaics, yet the role of epitaxial strain in controlling this process remains largely unexplored from first principles. We present a systematic firstprinciples study of strain-dependent hot-carrier cooling rates in six inorganic perovskiteshalides CsSnI3, CsSnBr3, and CsCaCl3, and oxides BaSnO3, BaZrO3, and KTaO3across a ±2% biaxial strain window. Eliashberg spectral functions ω2F (ε) are computed via density functional perturbation theory and Wannier interpolation, from which hot-carrier energy loss rates →dE/dt↑ are evaluated through the Fröhlich– EPW formalism for carrier temperatures up to 5000 K. Applying +1% tensile strain to BaZrO3 collapses the dominant-mode electron–phonon coupling constant from ϑ = 1.31 to ϑ = 0.011, suppressing the hot-carrier cooling rate by more than 90% relative to the least favorable strain condition and yielding a thermalization time ϖtherm = 1,585 fs and a hot-carrier figure of merit FOMHC = 1,348 fs, surpassing all halide configurations by more than an order of magnitude. Landau polynomial fitting of ε2 min (ϱ) confirms that no strain-induced structural phase transition occurs within ±2% for any compound, establishing a safe phonon engineering window. Orbital-projected densities of states reveal two mechanistically distinct coupling classes: gap-closure-driven coupling in BaSnO3 and CsCaCl3 [Spearman correlation ς(Eg, ϑ) ↓ ↔0.70] and purely phonon-mode-softening-driven coupling in BaZrO3 and KTaO3 (ς ↗ +0.72), the latter being invisible to band structure analysis alone.

Naveen Kumar, Anirban Mondal

item.title: Ordering-dependent subsurface reconfiguration reshapes the ORR activity ranking of L10 and L12 Pt–Fe nanoparticles
item.description:
Nanoparticle catalyst properties are often governed by activation-induced subsurface reconfiguration and ordering-dependent structural responses rather than nominal bulk phases. Static idealized models therefore can miss the kinetic pathways that drive subsurface evolution and active-site redistribution during synthesis and activation. Here, we present an activation-mapped kinetic modeling workflow combining density functional theory (DFT), machine-learning cluster expansion (ML-CE), Metropolis Monte Carlo (MMC), and kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) to trace processing-driven structural evolution in L1 0 and L1 2 Pt–Fe nanoparticles. We define the activation-derived ensemble as the statistically sampled Pt-skin configurations generated by high-temperature ordering, selective Fe leaching, vacancy-mediated restructuring, and room-temperature activation. This ensemble construction links processing history to subsurface composition, surface morphology, and site-resolved catalytic response. Within the modeled activation sequence, phase-dependent Fe leaching produces an inversion in second-layer Fe enrichment relative to the ideal ordered references and changes the dominant active-site families, making L1 0 -derived nanoparticles terrace-controlled, whereas L1 2 -derived nanoparticles become comparatively edge-controlled. When coupled to steady-state *OH coverage kinetics, these activation-derived ensembles recover the experimental oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity ranking and reveal phase-specific size–activity trends missed by ideal models. More broadly, the results show that the activation-derived structures, rather than pristine phases alone, govern catalyst ranking and highlight how ordering-dependent subsurface reconfiguration can reshape static-model predictions.

Jiadong Shen, Qi Xiao, Liang Cao

item.title: Adapting UMA to spin-polarized AQCat25 without catastrophic forgetting with task-gated LoRA
item.description:
Universal models for atoms such as UMA rival specialized interatomic potentials across chemistry [2], yet none of their catalysis datasets contains spin-polarized metallic surfaces [4, 9, 10]. On AQCat25 [1], a spin-polarized, higher-fidelity catalysis dataset, UMA loses accuracy where adsorption changes surface magnetization, and fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting [8, 13]. We add a task-specific mode to UMA through low-rank adapters (LoRA) [5] that act only on AQCat25 systems (0.065% of parameters). On unseen adsorbates and materials, the adsorption-energy error falls from 0.193 to 0.119 eV (−38%) and the force error from 0.091 to 0.031 eV/Å, with the largest gains on strongly magnetic systems. All seven original UMA tasks remain numerically unchanged, whereas full fine-tuning raised the OC20 error tenfold. EV2-in+midFiLM [3], the best model in the AQCat25 paper, reaches 0.268 eV on the same systems. Rather than predicting adsorption energies directly, UMA derives them from total energies, as the AQCat25 authors recommend for surfaces that restructure [1]. A foundation potential can thus gain a spin-aware, higher-fidelity mode without forgetting what it already knows.

Dejan Azul Ultamar

item.title: What topology hold-out removes—and what it does not
item.description:
Machine-learning screens of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for CO2 capture increasingly report the validation protocol that produced a score, and topology hold-out has become the standard stricter alternative to random splitting. Prior work already reads topology hold-out as a combined structural and chemical distribution shift; this work measures the size of the chemistry that the split withholds. On the hypothetical-MOF library hMOF (324,426 structures), 74.7% of coarse-grained chemical compositions occur in a single topology, accounting for 61.3% of structures, and seven of eleven topologies leave every structure without a chemical counterpart in training. On the one usable chemistry-matched pair (pcu ↔nbo), removing the partner topology raised nbo-side MAE by 70.0% while a size-matched control did not, and removing only the shared-composition partner rows improved pcu-side MAE, so partner coverage is direction-dependent rather than uniformly beneficial. A chemistry-key hold-out produces only 21.1% of the topology hold-out's R2 decrease, so the support loss is real but does not translate proportionally into performance loss. Across five independently redrawn 25,000-sample support sets, the top-1% hit rate fell from 50.4% to 19.3% under topology-grouped validation. A support audit in ARC-MOF, which is partly dependent on hMOF and uses different composition keys, confirms strong coupling under bounded sensitivity rather than as an independent replication. We retain topology hold-out as a stress test while recommending that groupedsplit reports disclose their chemical support, deployment-relevant aggregation and ranking performance.

Tao Wang

item.title: Structural evolution of the P2-Na2/3Ni1/3Mn2/3O2 sodium-ion battery cathode material resolved by 3D electron diffraction
item.description:
P2-Na2/3Ni1/3Mn2/3O2 is a promising cathode for sodium-ion batteries, yet its electrochemical behavior is governed by a complex sequence of structural transformations whose microscopic origins remain poorly understood. In particular, Na+/vacancy ordering is expected to play a central role in the phase evolution but is challenging to resolve using powder diffraction alone. Here, we combine continuous-rotation 3D electron diffraction (3D-ED) with operando and ex situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (SXRD) to establish a comprehensive structural picture of NaxNi1/3Mn2/3O2 across the full electrochemical window (1.0 V – 4.5 V). 3D-ED resolves Na+/vacancy ordering in sub-micrometer crystallites, revealing ordered P2 structures at Nax = 2/3, 1/2, and 1/3. In each case, Na+/vacancy ordering lowers the symmetry of the parent P2 framework and produces arrangements that minimize electrostatic repulsion while satisfying Pauling’s second rule. Transient phases at Nax = 3/5 and 2/5 are also observed during charging, while two highly sodiated P2 phases are accessed by discharging to low voltages. At high states of charge, extensive Na+ removal drives the P2→O2 transition and produces pronounced stacking disorder, demonstrating that the layer glide is not fully coherent. Bond-valence analysis further tracks transition-metal charge compensation during Na+ extraction. Together, these results establish Na+/vacancy ordering as a key structural variable governing phase stability, charge compensation, and structural transformations in P2-Na2/3Ni1/3Mn2/3O2, while highlighting 3D-ED as a powerful approach for resolving complex ordering phenomena in battery materials.

Hasindhi H. Lokuge, Kusalvin Dabare, Jason J. Zhou, Moinak Dutta, Mark Del Campo, Claire E. Casaday, Molleigh B. Preefer, Joshua D. Bocarsly

item.title: Spontaneous defect formation as the origin of superionic transitions in antifluorite-type structures
item.description:
Solid-state electrolytes offer the possibility of safer and higher energy density batteries, yet only a limited number of materials achieve ionic conductivities suitable for practical applications. Type-II superionic conductors, which undergo continuous temperature-driven transitions between low and high ionic conductivity regimes are strong candidates for high-performance solid state electrolytes, but the transition mechanism is not sufficiently understood. In this study, we investigate the archetypical superionic conductors Li2O and Li2S with the antifluorite structure using long-time-scale molecular dynamics simulations with an Allegro machine-learning force field (MLFF) trained on density functional theory data selected using an on-the-fly active learning procedure. To this end, superionic transitions are identified around 1450 K for Li2O and around 1100 K for Li2S through continuous peaks in the heat capacity. Diffusion coefficients and concentration of Frenkel defects are found to exhibit strong non-Arrhenius behavior coinciding with the superionic transition where both diffusion activation energy and defect formation energy decrease significantly across the transition. This suggests a self-enhanced spontaneous defect formation mechanism, which drives the superionic transition and promotes increased ionic diffusion. These results identifies the microscopic origin of type-II superionic behavior as a result of correlated defect formation and support the design of improved solid-state electrolytes.

Timothée Jamin, Kasper Tolborg

item.title: Complete stabilization of surface oxygen vacancies in high-entropy oxides
item.description:
High-entropy oxides retain a significantly larger population of oxygen vacancies (OVs) compared to their single-element or binary metal oxide counterparts, highlighting their unique potential as prospective electrocatalytic materials. However, the stabilization of surface oxygen vacancies (S-OVs) is highly challenging due to their inherently dynamic nature generally resulting in defect healing, migration, or initiation of structural collapse under operating conditions. By means of rational high-throughput materials science, we investigate the stability of S-OVs in (Cu-Fe-Ni-Cr-Zn)O x high-entropy oxides covering a compositional search space of at least 5 to 35 %. A methodology based on X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and X-ray absorption spectroscopy is utilized to quantitatively follow the distribution of the OVs across the materials library. For low Zn stoichiometries, (Cu 14 -Fe 13 -Ni 5 -Cr 8 -Zn 4 )O 55 , complete stabilization of S-OVs is achieved even after prolonged exposure to ambient environment. The discovery of S-OV stabilization in our high-entropy oxide system is a prerequisite to exploit the unique properties of this class of materials for electrocatalytic applications and beyond.

Johannes D. Bartl, Nophar Tubul Levy, Alina Sermiagin, Noa Levi, Sidharth Reghunathan, Bibhudatta Malik, Shany Myers, Adi Kama, Roberto Félix, Regan G. Wilks, Susan Nehzati, Marcus Bär, Hannah Noa Barad
